stories: You are the class leader, and your teacher steps out for a meeting. She says, "Write down the names of anyone who talks." The room slowly turns noisy, and when she returns, she asks for the list. Your best friend, who shares her lunchbox with you whenever you forget yours, is on it. Your pen stops moving. Your eyes sting, and you cannot tell whether you are more afraid of the teacher or of losing your friend's trust.

Your younger brother has been skipping his tuition to play cricket, and he has begged you not to tell. He has covered for you more than once. One evening your mother looks straight at you and asks, "Is he going to his class?" You remember your grandfather saying, "Boys don't cry," so you hold it in, and the lump in your throat only grows.

Your closest friend told his father he was at your house all Sunday, and he was not. Now his father is at your door, asking you kindly whether it is true. Your friend has stood by you since you were both six. You look at your feet, and your eyes fill, because you care about him and you cannot say yes.
helps: Let the feeling be real. Tears that come from caring are nothing to be ashamed of.
Say it to someone you trust. A parent, an elder, a coach, a close friend or a cousin can help you put it plainly: "I care about this person, and I have to do something hard."
Ask one question: "What is the honest and kind thing to do?"
Be firm without being cruel, because the person in front of you carries the same Self as you.
Try this today: Tell one trusted person about something that is weighing on your heart.
2.1.read: tam tathaa kripayaa-vishtam ashru-poorna-aakulekshanam | visheedantam idam vaakyam uvaacha madhusoodanah
2.1.meaning: Arjuna was filled with pity and sorrow, his eyes full of tears and his mind troubled. Then Krishna spoke to him.
2.1.bhakti: Krishna does not call Arjuna's tears wrong. He stays beside him. When love and duty pull in two directions, we can offer both to Him in prayer. The same God sits in the heart of the person we have to disappoint.

stories: You are to sing at the temple festival tomorrow, and you have practised the song for a month. Lying in bed, your mind fills with "What if my voice cracks? What if I forget the words?" By morning you tell your mother, "I don't want to go." She does not scold you. She sits beside you and asks softly, "Where is this coming from? I have heard you sing this very song every evening." Her question gives you a small gap in which to breathe.

You and your friend had a bad quarrel, and you have come to say sorry. At her gate, your hands are cold. "She will shut the door on me. She has already told everyone," you think, and you turn to leave. Your elder sister, who walked with you, says, "Is that something you know, or is it just the fear talking? Ring the bell." By the time the door opens, the fog has thinned.

The colony football match has come down to one penalty, and your friends want you to take it. A familiar thought returns: "Everyone here is better than me, and today they will see it." You ask if someone else could take it. Your friend says calmly, "We chose you because we have watched you score a hundred of these. Is this a fact, or just a feeling?" You place the ball and realise your feet know what to do.
helps: Pause and ask: "Is this a fact, or a fog?"
Take three slow breaths.
Remember one real proof of your effort, such as the practice you did, the song you learned or the goals you have already scored.
Tell someone who knows you, like a parent, a sibling or a close friend. They can often see your steadiness when you cannot.
Try this today: Before something big, say a short prayer: "Lord, be with me. I will do my part."
2.2.read: kutas tvaa kashmalam idam vishame samupasthitam | anaarya-jushtam asvargyam akeerti-karam arjuna
2.2.meaning: Krishna said, "Arjuna, how has this fog of confusion come over you at such a serious moment? Good people do not hold on to it. It will not lift you up, and it will not bring you a good name."
2.2.bhakti: Krishna's first words are a question, not a scolding, because He knows Arjuna's true nature is stronger than the fog. A short prayer before a big moment can bring that steadiness back.

stories: Your closest friend has stopped talking to you after a quarrel. You shut your door and tell your family, "I am never going out to play again." After a while your father knocks, sits beside you and says gently, "Wash your face. Then walk with me to the shop, and we will think about what you can do." It is hard to move, but you get up and splash water on your face, and for the first time that day you take a deep breath.

You have failed one subject and will have to write that exam again. You are sure everyone is talking about it, so you stop going to class. "What is the point?" you tell your friend. She does not argue. She says, "Come, let us have tea first. Then we will sit down and plan for the re-exam." Walking to the tea shop with her is your first step back.

Relatives are coming for lunch, and you have offered to make the payasam yourself for the first time. It burns, and the smell fills the house. "I will never cook again," you say, and you walk out of the kitchen. Your mother calls you back. "Everyone in this family has burned it once, including me. Wash the pot. We have time to make it again." You pick up the pot.
helps: Do one small act of standing up. Wash your face, drink water, step outside or message one person.
Make a simple plan for the next small step, with a cousin, a friend or an elder who has been through something similar.
Remember: feelings of failure are heavy, but they are not the whole of you.
Try this today: Write down one small thing you will do tomorrow morning.
2.3.read: klaibyam maa sma gamah paartha naitat tvayy upapadyate | kshudram hridaya-daurbalyam tyaktvottishtha parantapa
2.3.meaning: "Do not give in to this loss of spirit, Arjuna. It does not suit you. Shake off this small weakness of the heart and stand up."
2.3.bhakti: Krishna says "stand up" with great affection, and He believes in Arjuna before Arjuna believes in himself. The word translated as "unmanliness" really means loss of spirit, which can happen to anyone, and anyone can recover it with His grace.

stories: Your father taught you chess, one patient evening at a time. Today, in the final of the apartment tournament, he is sitting across the board from you. You see a move that will win the game, and your hand stops above the piece. It feels strange to defeat the person who taught you how.

Your elder sister taught you your first dance steps, and she still corrects your hands before every programme. This year both of you have tried for the same solo, and only one will get it. One small voice inside you is jealous of her, and another feels guilty for feeling that way. You wonder if dancing your very best against her is a kind of betrayal.

Your coach taught you everything you know about the game, and you owe him a lot. Before the big match he announces the batting order, and you can see a mistake in it: he does not know that one of your teammates is hiding an injury. You feel torn. Correcting him in front of the team seems disrespectful, but staying silent could cost everyone the match.
helps: Say thank you first. Before the moment, silently thank the person who taught you.
Do your honest best. Respect does not mean holding back or staying silent.
Speak kindly and politely. In the last case, you might say privately, "Sir, may I tell you one thing before we start?"
Notice jealousy without feeding it. It is a normal feeling. Remember that the same Self lives in them and in you, and try to be glad for what they have achieved.
Try this today: Send a thank-you message to a teacher or an elder who helped you.
2.4.read: katham bheeshmam aham sankhye dronam cha madhusoodana | ishubhih pratiyotsyaami poojaarhaav arisoodana
2.4.meaning: "Krishna, how can I fight Bhishma and Drona with my arrows in battle? They deserve my deepest respect."
2.4.gem: Same Self in all (respect, gratitude and healthy competition)
2.4.bhakti: The Gita never calls Arjuna's respect for his elders wrong. A grateful heart is part of devotion, and a good teacher carries a light that comes from God.

stories: You are the younger of two brothers, and all your life you have heard, "Why can't you be like him?" This year he sat up many nights helping you build your science model. At the exhibition a judge asks, "Did you do all this by yourself?" Your parents are standing right there. For once you could be the brother who is praised. But you remember him holding the torch while you fixed the wires at midnight, and the prize starts to feel empty before you have even won it.

Your elder sister sat with you every evening this year until fractions finally made sense. Now the two of you are fighting over who gets the bigger room, and your father will decide tonight. You know she came home late last week and did not tell him. One sentence from you would win the room. Then you look at your maths notebook, full of her handwriting, and you know you could never enjoy a room won that way.

You learned to sing from your elder sister, and now relatives keep comparing the two of you. At a family function you are to sing together. She has a sore throat today and asks for a song that sits low. You could insist on the one with the high notes, where your voice would shine and hers would break. You think, "Could I look her in the eye tomorrow?" You choose the song she can sing.
helps: Ask yourself: "Will I be able to enjoy this and look myself in the mirror tomorrow?"
Choose the smaller success that is honestly yours.
Share credit freely. Say out loud who helped you, and name them in front of others.
Be big-hearted with your brother or sister. A generous person gives the credit away and still feels rich.
Try this today: Thank, by name, someone who helped you recently.
2.5.read: guroon ahatvaa hi mahaanubhaavaan / shreyo bhoktum bhaikshyam apeeha loke / hatvaartha-kaamaams tu guroon ihaiva / bhunjeeya bhogaan rudhira-pradigdhaan
2.5.meaning: "It is better to live on simple food than to harm my noble teachers. If I harmed them, every pleasure I gained would be stained with the pain I caused."
2.5.gem: Mindful action (honesty, gratitude and sharing credit)
2.5.bhakti: Arjuna chooses gratitude over gain. A heart that stays thankful to its teachers is already close to God, because He lives in them too.

stories: Everyone is asking whether you will choose science, commerce or arts. Your friends have already decided, and you honestly do not know what you are good at. Your parents have suggested a direction based on what they see in you, and your teachers have their own views. You feel behind, as if everyone else was handed a map. You sit down with your parents and a teacher you trust, and together you look at your interests and strengths one at a time.

Two of your closest friends have quarrelled, and each wants you on her side. One says, "If you sit with her, don't talk to me." You have heard both stories, and both sound true. You turn it over again and again, and each time you end up exactly where you started, unable to tell who is right.

You are the captain, and there is one place left in the team for Saturday's final. Your closest friend has been out of form for a month, and a new boy is clearly playing better. If you pick your friend and the team loses, you have let down ten others. If you pick the new boy and the team wins, you will be holding the cup while your friend watches from the side, and you are not sure you would even enjoy it. Whichever way you turn, someone you care about is hurt. You cannot tell which choice is better, and at last you go to your coach and say so.
helps: Say it calmly: "I do not know yet, and that is okay."
List what you truly value, and talk to two or three trusted people, such as your parents, an elder in the family or a teacher.
Choose the next step, not your whole life.
Give it your best, and stay open to changing course.
Try this today: Write down three things you enjoy doing and three things people say you are good at.
2.6.read: na chaitad vidmah kataran no gareeyo / yad vaa jayema yadi vaa no jayeyuh / yaan eva hatvaa na jijeevishaamas / te 'vasthitaah pramukhe dhaartaraashtraah
2.6.meaning: "I do not even know which is better for us: to fight or not to fight, to win or to lose. The very people we would not want to live without are standing in front of us."
2.6.bhakti: Arjuna openly says, "I do not know." That honesty is where he begins to learn. We too can offer our confusion to God and ask, "Show me the next step."

stories: You are leaving for your master's degree in two months, and you do not know how to cook. You save forty cooking videos. One says to roast the rava first, another says never to, and a third needs an oven you will not have. After a week of burnt upma you lose interest and tell yourself you will manage on noodles. One evening you go into the kitchen and say, "Amma, I have watched everything, and I still cannot cook. Will you teach me?" She laughs and says, "One simple dish a day. Today, only rice and dal." The next day it is rasam, and the day after, a potato curry. By the time you pack your bags, you have ten dishes you can make without looking at a screen, written in your own notebook.

A group of boys has been teasing you for weeks. You have always believed that asking for help is a sign of weakness, so you have kept quiet. Finally you sit down next to your elder brother and say, "I am not sure what to do." He puts his phone away and says, "Good. Now we can actually start."

It is the hardest chapter in physics, and the class has been lost for a week. Each time the teacher asks, "Is that clear?" thirty heads nod, because nobody wants to be the only one who has not understood. Today she writes one simple problem on the board and asks who will solve it. Nobody moves. "You all nodded yesterday," she says. After a long silence one student stands up. "Ma'am, I have not understood anything since last Monday." Another says, "Me too," and soon half the class has said it. The teacher puts down the chalk and smiles. "Thank you. Now I know where to begin. A nod teaches me nothing, and it teaches you nothing either." She goes back to the first page, and this time the questions come from every bench.
helps: Choose one or two guides, such as a parent, a grandparent, a teacher or a senior, instead of listening to everyone.
Say it plainly: "I do not know. Please guide me."
Listen fully. Elders often carry lessons they learned the hard way, so hear them out before you decide.
Try what they suggest, and go back to tell them how it went.
Try this today: Write three questions for a person you respect, and ask one of them.
2.7.read: kaarpanya-doshopahata-svabhaavah / prichchhaami tvaam dharma-sammoodha-chetaah / yach chhreyah syaan nishchitam broohi tan me / shishyas te 'ham shaadhi maam tvaam prapannam
2.7.meaning: "My heart is heavy with helplessness, and my mind is confused about what is right. Please tell me clearly what is truly good for me. I am your student, and I have come to you for shelter. Please teach me."
2.7.gem: Mindful action (learning with an open heart, and respect for elders and teachers)
2.7.bhakti: Arjuna says, "I am your student, teach me." Asking for guidance with an open heart is itself a prayer, and the wisest teacher we meet carries a light from God.

stories: You score top marks, and everyone congratulates you. Your family is proud, and your phone is full of messages. That night, you lie awake feeling strangely empty. You think, "I have everything I wanted, so why do I feel like this?" You say nothing, because everyone has told you that you should be happy.

After a year of asking, you get the phone you wanted. For a week you are thrilled. Then you feel flat. You scroll for hours without enjoying anything, and you notice yourself comparing your phone with a friend's newer one. You tell yourself you have no right to complain, when your parents stretched to buy it.

For a whole year you wanted to be part of one particular group, and now they have made room for you. You sit with them and laugh at their jokes. On Sunday evening the same quiet heaviness returns. You find yourself missing the old friend you stopped sitting with, and already worrying about how to keep your place.
helps: Know that this is normal. A new thing or a big win feels exciting for a few days, and then the feeling fades. That does not mean you are ungrateful or that something is wrong with you. Every prize works this way.
Catch the thought, "I will be happy when I get..." You once thought it about the very thing you now have. The next thing will not fill the gap either, so you can stop chasing it.
Give instead of getting. Teach a younger child, help at home without being asked, or share what you have. Giving fills the place that getting cannot reach.
Spend ten quiet minutes a day on what fills you from the inside: a prayer, a song, a walk or time with a grandparent, with no screen nearby.
Say it out loud to a parent, a sibling or an elder you trust: "I got what I wanted, and I still feel empty." They have felt it too.
Try this today: Do one helpful thing for someone without telling anybody. At night, compare that feeling with how you felt on the day you last got something new.
2.8.note: If the heaviness stays for many days, talk to a family member you trust, such as a parent, a grandparent or an elder.
2.8.read: na hi prapashyaami mamaapanudyaad / yach chhokam uchchhoshanam indriyaanaam / avaapya bhoomaav asapatnam riddham / raajyam suraanaam api chaadhipatyam
2.8.meaning: "I cannot see anything that will take away this sorrow that is drying up my strength, even if I won a rich kingdom on earth with no rivals, or even became ruler over the gods."
2.8.gem: Evenness (what truly fills the heart: gratitude and contentment)
2.8.bhakti: Even a great warrior like Arjuna learned that no kingdom can fill the heart. The lasting fullness comes from within, from the Self and from God.

stories: After a lost match, an argument with a close friend and a scolding at home, you say to yourself, "I am done with everything." You stop answering messages and lie quietly in the dark. You have not decided anything. You just have no words left.

You and your sister have had a fight in which both of you said too much. You lock your door and lie on the bed. Your mother calls you for dinner three times, and you do not answer, because you do not know how to explain.

Your friends made a plan without you, and you found out from their photos. You mute the group, leave your phone inside and sit on the terrace, unable to reply to anyone. It feels as if it makes no difference whether you are there or not.
helps: Do not let things pile up. Arjuna went silent after one worry had settled on top of another. Talk about a small upset on the same day, while it is still small.
Make talking a daily habit. Tell one person at home one thing about your day, every day. Then, on a hard day, the door is already open.
Look after the basics: sleep, food, play and a short prayer. A tired, hungry mind goes dark much faster.
If you are already there, do one tiny thing. Drink water, step outside, and send one line to a friend, a sibling or a parent: "I am not okay right now."
Do not stay silent on your own for days. Go and sit with a parent, a grandparent or an elder you trust. You do not need the right words. "I do not know how to say it" is enough to begin.
Try this today: Tonight, tell one person at home one small thing that bothered you today.
2.9.read: evam uktvaa hrisheekesham gudaakeshah parantapa | na yotsya iti govindam uktvaa tooshneem babhoova ha
2.9.meaning: After saying this to Krishna, Arjuna said, "I will not fight," and became silent.
2.9.gem: My steady Self (silence is not the end)
2.9.bhakti: Arjuna's silence is not the end of the story, because Krishna waits right beside him. When you have no words left, a silent prayer is enough.

stories: You come home upset after a quarrel with a friend and sit quietly in your room. Your grandmother does not ask a hundred questions or give a lecture. She sits beside you, hands you a glass of warm milk and says, "Drink this first. Then we will talk." Her calm makes the problem feel a little smaller.

You were left out of the team, and you feel low. Your elder cousin, who went through the same thing a few years ago, calls in the evening. He does not tell you what to do. He says, "Tell me everything, I am listening." By the end of the call, you are laughing at something small.

Your younger brother comes home, throws his bag down and will not say what happened. You do not rush in with advice or questions. You sit beside him, peel an orange, pass him half and say, "Whenever you want to talk, I am here." Your calm gives him room to breathe.
helps: Let a calm person in, such as a grandparent, an elder you trust or a close friend.
When someone else is struggling, sit beside them and listen first. Sharing your time and calm is a gift.
Take three slow breaths before you speak to anyone who is upset.
Try this today: Offer to sit with someone who looks like they are having a hard day.
2.10.read: tam uvaacha hrisheekeshah prahasann iva bhaarata | senayor ubhayor madhye visheedantam idam vachah
2.10.meaning: Then, in the middle of the two armies, Krishna spoke these words to the sorrowful Arjuna, with a gentle smile.
2.10.bhakti: Krishna stays steady in the middle of Arjuna's storm. The same God lives in the heart of the person who is hurting, so when we sit calmly with them, we are keeping Him company too.

stories: You are the friend everyone calls for advice. When a classmate is teased about her voice, you tell her, "Their words don't decide who you are," and you mean it. Then someone laughs at your drawing, and you sulk for days, forgetting every word you said. Your elder sibling notices and asks, "What would you tell your friend if she were in your place?"

You comforted a friend when her best friend left her for another group. "You are worth more than this, and time will help," you said. A few months later, your own close friend drifts away, and you cannot hear those words at all. A cousin who knew about the earlier conversation gently reminds you, "You said the same thing to your friend, remember?"

When your little sister spills paint on her project, you tell her, "Mistakes are how we learn." Then you miss an easy goal in front of everyone and scold yourself for a week. She listens to you muttering and asks quietly, "Would you speak to me the way you are speaking to yourself?"
helps: Hear your own advice as if a friend were saying it to you.
Write down the kind words you give to others, and read them on a hard day.
Ask an elder sibling, a cousin or a close friend to remind you of them when you forget.
Try this today: Write one piece of advice you once gave someone, and read it to yourself.
2.11.read: ashochyaan anvashochas tvam prajnaa-vaadaamsh cha bhaashase | gataasoon agataasoomsh cha naanushochanti panditaah
2.11.meaning: Krishna said, "You are sad about things that do not need such sorrow, yet you speak words of wisdom. Wise people do not grieve over those who have gone or those who are still here."
2.11.gem: My steady Self (the wisdom is already in you)
2.11.bhakti: Krishna begins with honesty and affection. He sees the wise person in Arjuna before Arjuna does. The wisdom you give to others comes from the same Self within you.

stories: The group of friends you shared your lunch with starts leaving you out. It feels as if you have disappeared. At home, one of your parents sits with you and says gently, "You were you before this group, and you will still be you after it."

You trained for months for a place on the team, and you did not get selected. For a long time you thought of yourself as "the sports person," and now you feel like nobody. A grandparent or an elder sibling says, "Who you are is far bigger than a title or a team."

Your family moves to a new town. In the old one, everybody knew you as the singer, the one who made the whole class laugh. Here nobody knows your name, and you wonder who you are without all that. In the evening your father says, "Your talent, your values and your kindness came with us on the same train. They are still yours."
helps: Write a short list of who you are beyond one group, one result or one title. Include your values, your strengths and the people who love you.
Ask a parent, an elder or a friend to add to it.
Remind yourself each morning: "I am more than today's result."
Try this today: Add one thing to your list that no result or title can take away.
2.12.read: na tv evaaham jaatu naasam na tvam neme janaadhipaah | na chaiva na bhavishyaamah sarve vayam atah param
2.12.meaning: "There was never a time when I did not exist, or you, or all these people. And none of us will ever cease to be."
2.12.gem: My steady Self (always here, always held)
2.12.bhakti: Krishna says "I, you and all of these," which means every one of us has always been held in His presence. We are never truly alone, even when a group, a title or a place disappears.

stories: Next year you move to the senior school, and the thought makes your stomach tight. The building is bigger, the subjects are harder, and nobody there knows you. Your elder sister sits down beside you and opens three photographs: you at four with a missing tooth, you at nine in a cricket cap, and you last week. "Three different bodies," she says. "You were scared on your first day of school too, and that small body is long gone. Who walked in through the gate then, and who is about to walk into this one?" You say, "Me." "The same you," she says. "The body keeps moving to its next stage, and the one inside moves along with it. That is why a steady person does not panic at a change. And the God you folded your hands to in that first picture is already waiting at the new gate."

You have grown so fast this year that nothing fits, and your voice cracks in the middle of a sentence. Your friends laugh, and you feel like a stranger in your own body. Your father shows you a photograph of himself at your age, all elbows and knees. "Nothing of that boy's body is left," he says. "The height, the voice and the hair have all changed. But I remember being him, because the one inside never changed. It is the same with you. Your body is only moving to its next stage. The you who lives in it is exactly who you were last year, and God is looking after you now just as He did when you were a baby."

Your elder sister has left home for college, and her room is very quiet. Everything seems to be changing, and you say so to your grandmother on the phone. She laughs and says, "Open the old album. There I am as a baby, then as a schoolgirl in two plaits, then as a bride, then as a young mother, and now as your grandmother. Five bodies, and every one of them looks different. But who was inside every photograph?" You say, "You." "Me," she says. "The same me. Childhood, youth and old age were three changes of the body, and I went through each of them without ever becoming someone else. Krishna says the very same thing happens when this old body is finished: I will simply move on to the next body, as I moved on from being a girl. A steady person is not frightened by that. The Krishna I prayed to as a child is the Krishna I pray to today, and He is with you and your sister in this new stage too."
helps: See change as a stage, not a loss. Think of how much you have already changed since childhood, and notice that you are still you.

Ask, "Who has been here through all of it?" Look at an old photo and ask what has changed and what has not. The body, the voice and the likes have changed. The one looking out is the same. That is the real you, the Atma.
Keep one thing from each stage, such as a friend, a habit or a photo.
Welcome one new thing this week, like a new class, a new place or a new person. God is already there before you arrive.
Try this today: Find a photo of yourself from five years ago and say, "That was me, this is me, and God was with me in both."
2.13.note: **What this verse is telling you:** Childhood, youth and old age are changes of the body, and the one living in it, the Atma, goes through all of them without changing. The change after death is only the next one in the same line: the Atma takes another body. Once you see this, you are not bewildered by change, whether it is a new school, a new voice or the end of a long life.
2.13.read: dehino 'smin yathaa dehe kaumaaram yauvanam jaraa | tathaa dehaantara- praaptir dheeras tatra na muhyati
2.13.meaning: "Just as the one who lives in this body passes through childhood, youth and old age, in the same way it passes on to another body. A steady person is not troubled by this."
2.13.gem: My steady Self (change is natural, and I stay)
2.13.bhakti: The same "I" has been with you through every stage, and God has been with that "I" all along. He holds the child, the young person and the elder equally. Whatever stage comes next, you will not enter it alone.

stories: You post a video of a song you have practised for weeks, and a stranger leaves a mocking comment. It stings all evening, and you keep checking your phone to see if anyone else has said anything. A few days later, your cousin brings it up, and you have to think hard to remember what the comment said.

It is a hot afternoon, and your mother asks you to help clean the house before guests arrive. You would much rather lie down with your phone. The work is tiring and dull, and your first thought is to find a way out of it. But after a few minutes of starting, the discomfort fades, and by evening you feel proud that the house looks bright and your mother looks relaxed.

Your father scolds you sharply at nine at night for coming home late. Your stomach tightens, and you think about it all through dinner and for a long time in bed. The next morning he asks, "Shall I drop you at the bus stop?" as if nothing had happened, and you realise the sting lasted much longer in your mind than in his.

You are driving to your grandparents' village for the holidays. The highway ends, and the road becomes one pothole after another. The car crawls, the signal drops and the video you were watching freezes. You complain about the road, then about the network, then about the heat, for a full hour. Nothing improves. The road stays bad, the bars on your phone do not come back, and now everyone in the car is in a bad mood as well. Your grandfather turns around and asks, "Can you repair this road today? Can you put up a tower?" You shake your head. "Then the complaining only makes a rough road rougher. It will end in forty minutes whether you grumble or not." You put the phone away and look out of the window. The potholes are the same, but the journey is not. In the village the wifi is slow and the power goes off at eight, and you find you can let that be too. You play cards by lamplight with your cousins, and it becomes the evening you remember.
helps: Say, "This will pass." Heat and cold, pleasure and pain all come and go.

If you cannot fix it, do not feed it with complaints. A slow connection, an internet outage, a power cut or a bad road is not in your hands. If there is something you can do, do it. If there is not, complaining changes nothing outside and spoils the mood inside. Accept it, and find something else to do.
Take three slow breaths before you reply to anything that stings.
Do the next small task even while you feel uncomfortable. Many unpleasant things fade once you begin. Talk it over with a friend, a sibling or a parent if something still hurts after a day or two.
Try this today: Do one small task you have been avoiding, such as a chore at home, for just ten minutes.
2.14.read: maatraa-sparshaas tu kaunteya sheetoshna-sukha-duhkhadaah | aagamaapaayino 'nityaas taams titikshasva bhaarata
2.14.meaning: "The touch of the world on our senses brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and they go, and none of them lasts. So bear them patiently, Arjuna."
2.14.bhakti: Krishna calls Arjuna "Bharata", a member of a great family, as if to say, "You already have the strength to bear this." When we offer our discomfort to God, it feels lighter.

stories: Your cousins come to stay for the festival, and for four days the house is full of noise, games and sweets. You are on top of the world. Then they leave, the house goes quiet, and you sulk for three days and snap at everyone. Your mother takes you to the temple and sits with you on the steps of the tank. "Look at the water," she says. "Yesterday the sun shone on it, and this morning it rained, and it stayed just as deep underneath. Happiness and sadness are like guests. They arrive, they stay a while, and they leave. For four days a full house decided your mood, and for three days a quiet house decided it, so both times the guests were running you. Enjoy the full house with your whole heart, and when it goes quiet, do not let it pull you down. A steady person does not hand the keys of his mood to the guests. Be the lake, not the weather. The peace that comes from that does not leave when the guests do. That is what Krishna calls lasting peace."

You play brilliantly in the first match of the tournament and hear the cheers. In the second match, you drop an easy catch, and your mood sinks so low that you cannot eat dinner. An older player who has been at it for years tells you, "The best players stay steady after both a cheer and a mistake. I was not born that way. It took years of practice, and before every match I still say a small prayer: let me be the same whether I win or lose."

You and your brother play carrom every evening. When you win, you dance around the room and tease him. When you lose, you push the board away and say he cheated. One evening he says, "I don't mind losing to you. I mind playing with you." It strikes you that winning and losing are both turning you into someone you do not like.
helps: Picture a calm lake. When a high or a low arrives, close your eyes for a moment and see deep, still water. Sunshine and storm both show on the surface, and neither reaches the bottom.

Give your heart a place to rest. A few quiet minutes with God every day, on good days and bad, is what gives the lake its depth. Evenness grows with practice and with His grace, so do not expect it in a week.
Enjoy the good moments without boasting, and face the hard ones without sinking. Before you share good news or react to bad news, ask, "Will this matter next month?"
Learn from a steady person. Watch how a grandparent, a teacher or a senior behaves after both good days and bad days.
Try this today: The next time something good or bad happens, take one slow breath, picture the lake, and only then react.
2.15.note: **What this verse is telling you:** Happiness and sadness come and go like guests, and you cannot keep either one. A person who stays even through both, without being thrilled off the ground or crushed into it, finds a peace that does not depend on what is happening outside.
2.15.read: yam hi na vyathayanty ete purusham purusharshabha | sama-duhkha- sukham dheeram so 'mritatvaaya kalpate
2.15.meaning: "The steady person, who is not shaken by these feelings and stays the same in pain and in pleasure, becomes ready for lasting freedom."
2.15.bhakti: Evenness is a gift that grows with practice and with grace. A heart that rests in God is like a calm lake, which reflects both sunshine and storm without losing its depth. We do the practising, and He deepens the lake.

stories: You scroll through a classmate's holiday photos, new phone and party pictures, and feel that your own life is dull. But a picture shows only one moment. It does not show the long drive, the quarrel in the car or the homework waiting at home. What stays from any holiday is how people treated one another.

Your friends begin comparing brands: shoes, phones, watches. You feel the pressure to buy the latest thing, even though your family has to stretch to afford it. In a year those shoes will be worn out, and a newer phone will be in every shop. The evening you all got drenched cycling home in the rain will still make you laugh ten years from now.

A friend posts about a prize, a new bicycle and a trip, all in one month. You feel a sting of jealousy and wonder if you are falling behind. A post is a highlight, not a whole life. The same friend has dull days and bad days that are never posted. Your own steady habits, which nobody photographs, will take you further than one good month.
helps: Ask, "Is this passing or lasting?" A trend, a look or a number of likes passes. Honesty, learning and kindness last.
Spend your time and money on what lasts: your learning, your health and your friendships.
When jealousy comes, name it, and then wish the other person well. It loosens its grip.
Try this today: Write down one thing you enjoy that no one can see online, and be thankful for it.
2.16.read: naasato vidyate bhaavo naabhaavo vidyate satah | ubhayor api drishto 'ntas tv anayos tattva-darshibhih
2.16.meaning: "What is not lasting has no true existence, and what is truly real never ceases to be. Those who see the truth have understood the nature of both."
2.16.gem: My steady Self (what is passing and what lasts)
2.16.bhakti: Krishna teaches us to look for what truly lasts, and that search leads us to Him.

stories: You forget your lines in the school annual-day play, and a few students laugh. You feel that your confidence has been destroyed. At home, one of your parents says, "Your love for the stage did not leave the building with you. Show me what you will try next."

At a family gathering, a relative looks at you and your sister and says, in front of everyone, "She is the bright one." People laugh. You feel that one sentence has made you smaller. Later your mother sits with you and says, "A remark cannot take anything out of you. Everything you are is still here, and I know all of it."

You started a reading club in your colony for the summer. Ten children came in the first week and two in the third, and then it closed. You think, "I am no good at this." An elder you trust says, "The club ended. Your gift for bringing people together did not."
helps: List three things about yourself that the failure did not change, such as your kindness, your curiosity or your hard work.
Remember that setbacks happen to what you do, not to who you are.
Ask a parent, a sibling or a close friend to tell you what they still admire in you.
Try this today: Write one sentence that begins, "Even after this, I am still someone who..."
2.17.read: avinaashi tu tad viddhi yena sarvam idam tatam | vinaasham avyayasyaasya na kashchit kartum arhati
2.17.meaning: "Know that to be unbreakable, by which this whole world is filled. No one can destroy that which never changes."
2.17.bhakti: The presence of God within you cannot be taken away by anyone's remark or by any result.

stories: You said something unkind to a friend, and you have put off the apology for a week because you are afraid. What if he laughs, or walks away in front of everyone? Then you ask yourself what exactly could be hurt. Your face may go red, and your pride may sting for a minute. Those pass. The real you, the one Krishna calls the Self, cannot be scratched by a no. With that thought the fear loosens, and you walk across the ground. He looks relieved and says, "I am glad you came. Let's play."

Your grandfather is eighty-four, and he is the only one who knows the old family stories: the village, the flood, how he met your grandmother. For two years you have meant to record them, and every holiday you have said, "Next time." One day you notice that he walks more slowly than he did last year. A body does not last forever, and that is exactly why you cannot keep saying next time. On Sunday you sit beside him with your phone and say, "Thatha, tell me from the beginning." He talks for two hours, and you are glad you did not wait.

It is your turn to speak at the school assembly. Your knees are shaking, your palms are wet and your heart is thumping. Every part of you wants to say you are unwell. Then you notice something odd: you can watch your knees shake. The shaking is in the body, and the one watching it is perfectly still. "My knees are nervous," you tell yourself. "I am the one who knows they are nervous, and I am all right." You walk up with your knees still shaking and give the speech. Nothing in you has been harmed, and the next time the shaking is smaller.
helps: Ask, "What can really be hurt here?" Your body can get tired and your pride can sting, and both recover. The real you cannot be harmed at all, so fear has much less to threaten you with.
Watch the fear in your body. Notice the fast heartbeat or the shaky hands. You are the one watching, not the shaking.
Do not wait for "some day." Bodies and chances do not last forever. If something matters, begin it now.
Take the first small step today, and name your duty in one line, such as "Finish this assignment by Friday."
Try this today: Set a ten-minute timer and start one thing you have been putting off because you are afraid.
2.18.read: antavanta ime dehaa nityasyoktaah shareerinah | anaashino 'prameyasya tasmaad yudhyasva bhaarata
2.18.meaning: "These bodies come to an end, but the Self that lives in them is eternal, cannot be destroyed and cannot be measured. So, Arjuna, rise and do what must be done."
2.18.gem: Mindful action (do what must be done, without fear)
2.18.bhakti: Krishna gives this instruction with love, as if to say, "What you truly are is safe with Me. Now do your part." Fear does not get the last word.

stories: In an argument, a friend calls you useless, and you carry that word for days as if it were the truth about you. Then you remember that last month the same friend called you the best friend he had. Neither word changed what you are.

You and your sister tease each other all the time. One evening you laugh at her singing in front of your cousins and call her a crow. She laughs too. Weeks later you notice that she has stopped singing at home, and you realise the "joke" stung more than you thought. Your grandmother has a way of putting it: the God we light the lamp for in the pooja room lives in your sister too. You would never call Him a crow. That evening you ask her to sing, and this time you listen properly.

You are late and irritated, and when your mother reminds you about your lunch, you snap, "You don't understand anything!" She says nothing and goes on packing it. All day the words sit badly with you. Every morning you fold your hands before the picture of God on the shelf, and it strikes you that the same Lord lives in the person who packed your lunch. The Self in her is untouched by your words, just as yours is untouched by other people's. That is no excuse for throwing them. It is the reason to speak to her with respect. You go home and say sorry before she can ask about your day.
helps: Remember who lives in the other person. Before you speak, think, "God is in this person too." Namaste means "I bow to the Lord in you." It is hard to be rude to someone you have just bowed to.
Remember that words describe a moment, not your core. What others say about you does not decide who you are.
Choose your own words with care. Ask, "Would I say this in front of God?" He is listening from inside the other person.
If you hurt someone, say sorry simply, and mean it.
Try this today: Before you speak to one person at home, say a silent namaste to the Lord in them. Then notice how your words come out.
2.19.read: ya enam vetti hantaaram yash chainam manyate hatam | ubhau tau na vijaaneeto naayam hanti na hanyate
2.19.meaning: "One who thinks the Self can kill, and one who thinks it can be killed, are both mistaken. The Self neither kills nor is killed."
2.19.bhakti: God lives within every person, untouched, including the one we hurt. Speaking kindly is a way of respecting Him. Our words cannot damage the Self in anyone, but they do show whether we remembered who is there.

stories: Your grandmother, who used to wait for you with warm food after school, has passed away. The house feels very quiet, and you do not know where to put your grief. Your mother holds you and says, "Cry as much as you need. Her body had grown old and tired, and it has stopped. But the one who loved you from inside that body was never born and never dies. She is safe with God, and her love has not gone anywhere."
helps: Allow the grief. Tears are a way of love.
Keep their memory alive with a prayer, a lamp, a favourite story or their favourite food.
Be with family, or call a cousin, an elder or a friend, and share stories.
Try this today: Tell one story about someone you love and miss.
2.20.read: na jaayate mriyate vaa kadaachin / naayam bhootvaa bhavitaa vaa na bhooyah / ajo nityah shaashvato 'yam puraano / na hanyate hanyamaane shareere
2.20.meaning: "The Self is never born and never dies. It has always been and always will be, ancient and unchanging. It is not destroyed when the body is."
2.20.bhakti: The Gita says that what is truly us is never lost. We can hold those we love in prayer, and their kindness continues to live in us.
2.20.star: This is Krishna's clearest description of the Atma. It was never born and it never dies, it is always the same, and it is untouched even when the body comes to an end. Almost the same words are found in the Katha Upanishad. Every other verse about the Self in this chapter explains this one.

parts.title: Part 1: Arjuna's sorrow (2.1–2.10)
parts.intro: Arjuna stands between two armies, overwhelmed by love, duty and fear. These ten verses are about what that feels like and how to begin finding your way.

parts.title: Part 2: Who am I, really? (2.11–2.30)
parts.intro: Krishna's first teaching is about who you really are. Your body, your moods, your marks and your roles keep changing. The one inside who is aware of all of them, the Atma, does not change and cannot be harmed, and the same Atma lives in everyone.

sk.2.3:
क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते ।
क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप ॥
sk.2.4:
कथं भीष्ममहं सङ्ख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन ।
इषुभिः प्रतियोत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन ॥
sk.2.5:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान्
श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके ।
हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव
भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान् ॥
sk.2.6:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो
यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः ।
यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषामस्
तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः ॥
sk.2.7:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः
पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसम्मूढचेताः ।
यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मे
शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम् ॥
sk.2.8:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्
यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् ।
अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धं
राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥
sk.2.9:
एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप ।
न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह ॥
sk.2.10:
तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः ॥
sk.2.12:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः ।
न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम् ॥
sk.2.13:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा ।
तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ॥
sk.2.15:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ ।
समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते ॥
sk.2.16:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः ।
उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः ॥
sk.2.17:
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम् ।
विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित्कर्तुमर्हति ॥
sk.2.18:
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः ।
अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत ॥
sk.2.19:
य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम् ।
उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते ॥
sk.2.20:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्
नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो
न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥

ONE.2.1: Krishna lets Arjuna's tears be seen before He says a word. Caring enough to cry is not weakness.
ONE.2.2: Fear and confusion are a fog that has come over you. They are not who you are.
ONE.2.3: Stand up. This heaviness is real, but it is not all of you.
ONE.2.4: Arjuna asks how he can fight the very teachers he respects most.
ONE.2.5: A win that comes from hurting the people who guided you is not worth having.
ONE.2.6: Arjuna admits he does not know what is right, and it is honest to say so.
ONE.2.7: Arjuna stops arguing and asks to be taught. Asking for help is where learning begins.
ONE.2.8: No prize, however big, can fill an ache on the inside.
ONE.2.9: Arjuna runs out of words and goes silent. Silence is not the end of the story.
ONE.2.10: Krishna smiles in the middle of the battlefield. His calm says the storm is not as big as it feels.
ONE.2.11: You already have the wisdom you give to others. Use it on yourself.
ONE.2.12: You have always been you, and you always will be. No group, title or result can change that.
ONE.2.13: Life moves from one stage to the next, and the same "you" goes through all of them.
ONE.2.14: Pleasant and unpleasant feelings both come and go. Bear them patiently, and they pass.
ONE.2.15: Be like a deep, calm lake that shows both sunshine and storm and stays still underneath. That steadiness is the way to lasting peace.
ONE.2.16: Much of what feels so important today is only passing. Look for what truly lasts.
ONE.2.17: Something in you cannot be broken by any failure or any remark.
ONE.2.18: The body does not last forever, and the real you cannot be harmed. So do not wait, and do not be afraid. Do what must be done.
ONE.2.19: A word cannot harm what you truly are. The same Self lives in every other person, and God lives there too, so speak to each one with respect.
ONE.2.20: What is truly us is never lost, even when someone we love leaves this world.

NEXT.2.4: Your respect for your teachers is good. Krishna will show Arjuna how to keep it and still do his duty.
NEXT.2.5: Krishna will show Arjuna how to act with a clear conscience.
NEXT.2.6: Krishna will show Arjuna the next step, not the whole road.
NEXT.2.7: Krishna begins His teaching only after Arjuna humbly asks. Everything that follows opens from this one step.
NEXT.2.8: Krishna will now turn Arjuna's eyes inward.
NEXT.2.9: Krishna is still right there in the chariot. He does not leave when Arjuna goes silent.

TITLE.2.15: Steady on good days and bad

INDEX: Nerves before an exam, interview or presentation
Friendship trouble and being left out
Choosing a stream, a course or a job
Too much advice, and asking for help
Change, moving and new stages of life
Losing a place, a role or a title
Being there for someone who is upset
gems: My steady Self (the Atma): my body, my moods and my marks keep changing. The one inside who is aware of them all does not change and cannot be harmed. That is the real me, the Atma. Knowing this is the root of resilience.
Evenness: feelings come and go, and I do not have to be thrown by them.
Mindful action: I give my full attention and best effort, and let go of the result.

Same Self in all: the same Atma, the one supreme consciousness, is alive in every person, just as the same electricity lights every lamp in the house. When I remember this, kindness, gratitude, sharing and a big heart come naturally, and jealousy has less to hold on to.

atma.title: First, what is the Atma?
paras: Try this for ten seconds. Look at your hand. You can see it, so you are the one who sees, and the hand is what is seen. Now notice your mood. You can tell whether you are cheerful or grumpy, so you are the one who notices, and the mood is what is noticed. Try it with a thought. Your body, your moods and your thoughts keep changing all day, and someone in you is quietly aware of every one of them. That someone is the real you. Sanskrit calls it the Atma. In this book we call it the Self.

A picture to keep. A bulb, a fan and a speaker look nothing alike, yet the same electricity runs all three. Without it they are only glass, metal and plastic. Your body is like the gadget, and the Atma is like the current. You cannot see it, but it is what makes the eyes see, the ears hear and the mind think. And just as one current runs every gadget in the house, the same Atma, the one supreme consciousness, is alive in every person you meet.

Three things Krishna says about it. It does not change: look at a photo of yourself at five, and you will find a different body, a different voice and different likes, with the same you looking out. It cannot be hurt: words, marks and failures reach the body and the feelings, and they never reach the Atma. And it is the same in everyone, which is why nobody is above you and nobody is beneath you.

You do not have to understand all of this today. In the next twenty verses Krishna gives one picture after another for it. As you read, keep asking one question: who is the one in me that notices all this?
